analysis.one_liner: Bars pharmacy benefit managers and insurers from also owning pharmacies, forcing them to divest.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, the biggest companies that decide which drugs your plan covers and what you pay for them also own the very pharmacies you fill them at. This bill would make that arrangement illegal. Companies that own a pharmacy benefit manager or a health insurer would have one year to sell off any pharmacy business, and federal antitrust agencies, state attorneys general, and private citizens could sue to enforce the split. It would also let regulators review and block future deals that would put a pharmacy back under the same roof as an insurer or PBM.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients paying prescription drug costs, since the bill's findings say dominant PBMs steer prescriptions to their own pharmacies and raise drug costs; independent pharmacies, which the findings tie to more than 7,000 closures between 2019 and 2024; and taxpayers and health plan enrollees, whom the findings say lose money when conglomerates shift profits into unregulated pharmacy segments to evade Medical Loss Ratio limits [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for one entity to own both a pharmacy and an insurance company or PBM, and requires violators to divest their pharmacy within one year of enactment [S2].

It gives the FTC and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division joint authority to enforce the separation, impose divestment milestones, and escrow 10 percent of a violator's profits each month until the deadline is met [S2].

It lets federal agencies, state attorneys general, and private individuals sue violators, with courts able to award triple damages to individuals and to order disgorgement of pharmacy revenues into an FTC fund used for consumers who were overcharged [S2].
It requires divestitures to be reported to the FTC and DOJ for antitrust review and lets those agencies block any follow-on transaction that would recreate the conflict or harm competition [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large vertically integrated health conglomerates — companies whose PBM, insurance, and pharmacy arms processed more than 90 percent of U.S. prescriptions in 2023, per the bill's findings — would have to sell off their pharmacy businesses within a year or face escalating penalties, including monthly escrow of 10 percent of profits and court-ordered divestiture by a trustee [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large health conglomerates owning PBMs and pharmacies

drawbacks.text: The one-year divestment deadline is aggressive for businesses this large — splitting pharmacy operations away from conglomerates like the ones described in the bill's findings could be disruptive to operations, employees, and continuity of patient care in the interim.

The 10-percent-of-profits monthly escrow penalty accrues automatically for missing milestones and is forfeited to the FTC fund if divestment misses the deadline, a sanction that could be challenged as disproportionate and could tie the enforcement agencies up in litigation for years.

The bill requires divestiture but does not dictate who may buy the divested pharmacies; a sale to another large chain rather than independent owners could leave pharmacy markets concentrated even after the ownership conflict is removed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — breaking a conflict of interest the FTC has already identified as a driver of higher drug prices and pharmacy closures — is real and large, and the enforcement design (escrow, disgorgement, private lawsuits) gives it teeth most antitrust bills lack. The main risks are the speed and rigidity of the one-year divestment clock for businesses this size, and the possibility that divested pharmacies are bought by other large chains rather than independents, which would change who holds market power without much changing the market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up.

narrative.text: H.R. 8779, the 'Patients Before Monopolies Act,' was introduced in the House on May 13, 2026 [S1].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large vertically integrated health conglomerates the bill would force to divest their pharmacies remain untouched; the bill sits without committee action, which preserves the status quo they benefit from.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Vertically integrated health conglomerates, so far

sides.party_line_note: The bill's eight cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans, so it has support from both parties, but no committee action has followed.

industries.note: PBMs would be barred from common ownership with any pharmacy, forcing the largest PBMs — which the bill's findings say processed more than 90 percent of U.S. prescriptions — to divest their mail-order, specialty, and retail pharmacy businesses. Their leverage over independent pharmacies and their ability to steer prescriptions to affiliates would end.

Insurers that own pharmacies would have to divest them, and the bill targets the transfer-pricing practice the findings describe, in which insurance units shift profits into unregulated pharmacy segments to evade Medical Loss Ratio limits. That practice currently works against enrollees and taxpayers.

The bill's findings tie the closure of more than 7,000 pharmacies between 2019 and 2024 to pressure from dominant PBMs; structural separation and the loss of affiliated competitors' self-preferencing would directly ease that pressure. Independent pharmacies gain customers and fairer contract terms.

Divested pharmacy businesses become saleable assets, and buyers could include pharmacy chains, grocers, or private equity; the bill requires FTC and DOJ review of any acquisition to keep it from recreating the conflict, but the eventual ownership of thousands of divested stores is an open question.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has 8 cosponsors (5 Democrats, 3 Republicans) and sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing, markup, or floor action scheduled. As a single-sponsor bill with modest cosponsorship referred to committee and no movement since introduction, the typical path at this stage is to remain in committee for the rest of the Congress unless the committee takes up PBM legislation broadly.
